guideIntro.message: This guide tells you what the extension adds to Twitch and how to use it, in the order you will meet it. Everything works as soon as you reload a Twitch page, with nothing to configure — and everything can be adjusted, or switched off, from “Settings” just below.

guideHoverTexte.message:
Leave the pointer on a channel for a moment: a window opens beside it, with the live video, the full title, badges and the timeline of what happened earlier.
• It works everywhere in the sidebar: followed channels, recommendations, Top Channels.
• No ads in the preview. The stream you open afterwards is left untouched.
• Too heavy? In “Settings”: its width, the stream quality, or the preview without video.

guideDureeTitre.message: How long they have been live

guideDureeTexte.message:
Under the viewer count, every card shows how long the stream has been live, kept up to date without opening the channel.
• A stream that stops shows “Ended” while its card leaves the list.
• Three formats to choose from in “Settings”: 4h19, 4:19 or 259 min.

guideBadgesTexte.message:
In the preview, badges give the context at a glance. Here they all are; each colour has a single meaning.
• Red: Twitch's content labels — mature games, violence, gambling… You know before you watch.
• Lime green: news — the channel just switched category, or came back after a drop. It fades after ten minutes.
• Blue, purple, grey: the co-stream — who hosts it, who else is live, who is in it without streaming.
• Gold: your subscription, and what comes next; pale gold: a subscription that has ended.
• Green, orange, pink: the stream's sponsor, a Hype Train under way, a discounted subscription.
• No colour: a note from Twitch, carried over as is.
• Rainbow: a subathon, and its day.

guideFriseTexte.message:
Walking in halfway through an eight-hour stream? The preview's timeline shows what happened before: one band per category, to scale, and the list underneath.
• “×3”: the streamer came back to that category three times.
• A channel that does not archive its streams? The timeline is rebuilt from the clips, and says so.
• A “~” before a duration, a colour that fades: the exact time is not known. Nothing is made up.

guideSubathonTexte.message:
A subathon is that stream subscriptions keep extending without end — days, sometimes weeks.
• A pill to the right of the username says which day the event is on; the preview badge repeats it.

guideCostreamTexte.message:
A steady coloured bar on the left edge of the card: this channel is streaming with others, one colour per co-stream. Several members in a row in the list share a single bar.
• On hover, the blue badge says who is hosting — “Host Stream”, or “Co-stream of …”; the purple one names members live outside your list; the grey one, those who are part of it without streaming.
• A sort groups them at the top of the list (chapter $1).
• The small “▶” cursor on the bar opens their streams together, in the multistream room — next chapter.

guideSalleTexte.message:
The “▶” cursor on a co-stream's bar opens its streams side by side, on the page.
• Hover it: it says what it opens — “Watch all 3”. Faces at its end? Members you do not follow: move onto them to add them. Shift+click opens the whole co-stream straight away.
• Click a tile to give it the sound — keys 1 to 6 work too — and the chat follows the sound. Without Shared Chat, tabs above the chat show another one without changing the sound.
• Six streams at most on screen: the others wait below, and a click brings them in.
• The streams line themselves up on their common sound, in about a minute of listening; with no common sound, nothing moves. “Automatic alignment” can be switched off in “Settings”.
• The room earns no channel points, and Twitch's ads play there as anywhere else.
• To close it: Escape, or a click on the cursor, now a “■”.

guideDebutTexte.message:
A red bar beating on the left edge of a card: that stream started less than ten minutes ago. It goes out on its own.
• The streamer drops and comes back within ten minutes? The bar does not light up again, and the uptime keeps counting the whole stream, outage included.
• Their preview then says “Back after a drop” for ten minutes, and its timeline shows where the stream cut out.

guideAboTexte.message:
The channels you subscribe to are in gold in the list.
• Nothing to do: while you are signed in to Twitch, the extension reads your subscriptions page every six hours by default. A brand-new subscription? Open the channel, or click “Sweep now” in “Your data”, under “Subscriptions”.
• On hover, the badge says how many months you have supported the channel, then what comes next: “Next anniversary” if it renews, “Expires in …” if it is about to end — a gifted sub, or one you no longer renew.
• Once the subscription has ended, the gold goes out and the badge says “Former sub”.
• Paid, gifted or mobile: all three count.

guideTriTexte.message:
Six buttons at the top of the list reorder it:
• Viewers — Twitch's own order.
• Subscriptions — yours first, with their number, offline ones included, on a pill.
• Personal popularity — from your own visits, kept on your machine.
• Stream uptime — the newest streams first, to catch beginnings.
• Alphabetical — by username.
• Co-streams — grouped at the top.
Below, two filters: category and language. They only offer what your channels are streaming right now.
• Buttons you do not use can be removed in “Settings”.

guideTopTexte.message:
The “Top Channels” tab, at the top of the sidebar, swaps your followed channels for the most-watched channels on all of Twitch, live — thirty by default, ten or fifty if you prefer.
• Pick a category or a language in the filters: you get its real ranking.
• Preview, uptime, badges, co-streams: these are cards like any other.
“Followed Channels” takes you back; your list has not moved.

guideViteTexte.message:
Twitch takes two to four minutes to show a channel that goes live, and keeps one that stops for five to ten. The extension refreshes the sidebar itself, every thirty seconds: viewers, category, uptime, arrivals and departures.
• Your followed channels are always fully unfolded: no more “Show more” to click.
• Hype trains, discount banners, sponsor strips and empty sections leave the sidebar; what they said comes back as a badge in the preview (chapter $1).
• Your watch streak and Twitch's stories row are tucked into the filter block, at the top of the list. Prefer them as Twitch shows them, or hidden? That is in “Settings”.

guidePanneauTexte.message:
Six groups, on the left:
• “Get started” — this guide, readable even with no Twitch tab open.
• “Settings” — everything the extension lets you choose.
• “Schedule” — your followed channels' streams, past, live and scheduled, with their replays; that is the next chapter.
• “Your data” — what it has remembered: the channels you visit most, at what times, your subscriptions, the channels it knows.
• “Diagnostics” — only useful when something goes wrong; it can be hidden in the settings.
• “Top Channels” — the state of the ranking and its categories.
Every section other than this guide reads the frontmost Twitch tab; without one, they say so.
• Something wrong? “Export a report” writes a text to read before sending it: counts, no lists — neither your channels nor your subscriptions.
• “Erase history” erases everything the extension has remembered, for good; your settings stay.

guideAgendaTexte.message:
The “Schedule” group does for all your followed channels at once what a channel's schedule page does on Twitch for just one.
• “The week”: day by day, past streams with their replay — one click opens it —, live ones, and the ones channels have scheduled. It opens on today, with the past days above; a stream that runs past midnight stays on the day it started.
• The arrows change week, up to eight back and two ahead; “Today” brings you back to the day itself, and the menu keeps a single channel.
• “Offline”: every channel that is not live — first those that have scheduled their next stream, the soonest on top, then the others, the most recently gone first. When it streamed, its replay one click away, and its next stream. “Their week” opens the week of its last stream. A channel Twitch no longer serves — account suspended, renamed or closed — does not vanish from it: it stays at the bottom, “Unavailable on Twitch”.
• “Subs only” and its padlock mark, before you even click, a replay reserved for the channel's subscribers when the extension doesn't know you're subscribed; subscribed, nothing shows: it is open to you.
The channels are all those you follow. Since Twitch's sidebar shows only a hundred, the extension rereads the full list on your Following page, in an invisible frame, every twelve hours. A replay exists only if the channel keeps its broadcasts, and for as long as Twitch keeps them; a scheduled stream, only if it keeps its schedule on Twitch. “No replay” only gets a day if the extension saw that stream live: Twitch only gives its end. The schedule asks nothing of Twitch until you open it.

guideVieTexte.message:
• No third-party server: the extension only talks to Twitch, through the public API the page already uses.
• Those calls are anonymous: no session token, no cookie. They cannot be tied to your account.
• One exception, said out loud: to know your subscriptions, the extension opens YOUR twitch.tv/subscriptions page in an invisible frame — every six hours by default, or as your setting says, sooner only after a sweep that found nothing or when you ask, and never when you are signed out. Your browser authenticates it as if you had clicked the link; the extension neither reads nor passes on your token.
• Your visits, your subscriptions and their tenure stay in your browser. Clear twitch.tv's site data, and nothing is left.
• No permission requested, no tracker, no telemetry. The extension only runs on twitch.tv.

descOptions.message: What the extension adds, and what it leaves alone. Everything is on by default; a purple dot marks what you changed.

descSemaine.message: Your followed channels' streams, day by day: past ones with their replay, live ones, and scheduled ones.

optDescApercuVideo.message: Off, the preview keeps its thumbnail, badges and timeline — it simply stops loading the video.

optDescApercuQualite.message: Applies to the next preview, no reload needed.

optDescSalle.message: A “▶” cursor, in the middle of a co-stream's bar, opens its streams together, on the page — on the bar of several channels as on that of a channel alone from its co-stream in the list. On hover, it stretches and says what it opens; the faces of those you don't follow appear beside it — move onto them, or Shift+click: the whole co-stream. Off: no cursor, no room; the bars stay.

optDescSalleAuto.message: The streams are synced by their shared sound — each stream's lips on its voice as you hear it. It takes about a minute of listening; without shared sound, nothing moves. Off: nothing moves on its own.

optDescAbonnes.message: "Subtle" keeps the colour and drops the shimmer. "None" gives the card back to Twitch.

optGrpListe.message: The list, its sorts and filters

optDescTopN.message: Above thirty, some languages lose an optimisation and the ranking takes longer to fill.

optDescStories.message: "Integrated" tucks Twitch's stories row into the filter block, with the number of channels with unseen stories. Always hidden in Top Channels mode.

optDescSerie.message: "Integrated" tucks Twitch's "Save your streak" row into the filter block, with the streak count. Always hidden in Top Channels mode.

optDescTheme.message: "Auto" follows Twitch's theme. Forcing one only changes how the extension paints on top.

optDescPanneauTheme.message: Separate from the one above: this panel has to paint itself with no Twitch tab open.

optDescPanneauDiag.message: The measurement chapters — lag, cycles, preview, switches — are only there to report a problem.

optDescPurge.message: Each button erases only its own memory. The red button at the bottom erases all of them.

purgeVisitsText.message: The "personal popularity" sort and the rhythm grid will start from zero. Subscriptions and followed channels are untouched.

purgeSubsText.message: The gold will leave the cards until the next sweep. Your visits and followed channels are untouched.

purgeRosterText.message: The list will rebuild itself by watching the sidebar. Your visits and subscriptions are untouched.

optResetTitle.message: Reset every setting to its default?

optResetText.message: All twenty-one settings on this page will return to their original value. Your data — visits, subscriptions, followed channels — is untouched.

extActionTitle.message: Cowlor's Sidebar — your data and your settings

guideRoueTexte.message:
A ⚙️ gear sits to the right of the sidebar title. One click opens this panel on top of Twitch, without leaving the page.
• The extension icon, in the browser toolbar, opens the same panel.
• To close it: the Escape key, or a click outside.

guideReglagesTexte.message:
“Settings” controls everything this guide presents. Nothing is imposed: what bothers you switches off, and a purple dot marks what you changed.
• Preview too heavy? Lower the quality, or cut the video: it keeps its thumbnail, its badges and its timeline.
• Gold too loud? “Subtle” keeps the colour and drops the shimmer.
• The multistream room and its automatic alignment switch off separately.
• The subscriptions sweep can be spaced out to once a day.
• Each memory — visits, subscriptions, known channels — can be erased on its own.
• Your settings export and import; one button restores them all.
